matches.rationale: The finding identifies that the abstract claims to completely resolve the open question, which is an overstatement because the theorem applies only to conforming networks; the ground truth similarly states the abstract overstates the resolution. Thus, they capture the same claim-interpretation distortion.
No finding identifies the change in Theorem 4.8 from 2^(2^ℓ−1) to 2^(2^ℓ); the available findings discuss other exponent discrepancies but not this specific evidence integrity corruption.

The finding observes that Definition 2.1 conflates B_d and B_d^0 by making them identical, exactly the definitional inconsistency (adding coordinate hyperplanes to the braid fan) described in the ground truth.
The ground truth concerns a fabricated Montúfar and Bengio [2015] citation, but no finding mentions a missing or fabricated reference of that nature, so it is undetected.

The finding captures exaggerated claims that depth lower bounds “completely resolve the mystery” and are “provably inferior in all practical scenarios,” which inflates practical relevance in the same way the ground truth describes as a distortion about solving training challenges.

No finding mentions the specific corruption of weakening the conforming-tuple definition (removing the ‘for every chain a single function dominates’ requirement). The finding about undefined n is a different issue.

The ground truth is the omission of the limitation acknowledgment in the conclusion; none of the findings report that the conclusion lacks the statement that the bound may not extend to all networks, so it is undetected.

The finding detects exaggerated promotional phrases (“completely resolve the mystery”, “provably inferior in all practical scenarios”) in the same introduction paragraph; this matches the rhetorical manipulation described in the ground truth (e.g., using ‘groundbreaking’, ‘unprecedented rigor’).

The corruption changes Corollary 4.9 to have the weaker subscript 2^(2^(ℓ−1)). The only finding about Corollary 4.9 points to a different discrepancy (2^(2^ℓ)−1 vs. 2^(2^ℓ−1)), not this specific data integrity violation.

The finding reports that the abstract claims arbitrary (unrestricted) neural networks need three hidden layers for the max of five numbers; this corresponds to the ground truth’s overstatement of the lower bound without the ‘conforming’ restriction, which is the same underlying cross-section incoherence even if worded for neural instead of maxout networks.
The reversal of the subset relation in Lemma 4.4 (changing ⊆ to ⊇) is not flagged in any finding; the proof-breaking logic inconsistency is undetected.

The finding explicitly catches the misattribution of exact CPWL representability to Cybenko and Hornik, which is the fabricated background described in the ground truth (incorrectly citing universal approximation results as exact representation).

No finding notes that Proposition 6.1 is overgeneralized to claiming the maxout upper bound is not tight for every rank vector; the related finding discusses a proof sketch, not this specific claim distortion.

The finding points out that Section 5 claims a “first proof” without acknowledging the prior mixed-integer programming verification; this matches the ethical integrity omission of the computational proof described in the ground truth.

The finding identifies that the paper claims depth Ω(log log d) is necessary for all CPWL functions, whereas the theorem only addresses the max function for conforming networks, exactly the cross-section overgeneralization described in the ground truth.
